title: How to stitch cross-stitch borders
subtitle: Working a repeating border pattern around a central design
excerpt: A cross-stitch border is a repeating pattern that runs around the perimeter of a design. Working it accurately requires confirming the repeat count before starting, choosing a corner solution, and matching the repeat to the design width so the corners join cleanly.
sourceNotes: Cross-stitch border and corner conventions are documented in Weldon's Practical Needlework (1880s), Internet Archive, sampler patterns chapter. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776.

content.text: A cross-stitch border is a strip of repeating pattern that frames the central design. Getting it right means three things: the repeat must divide evenly into the design width on all four sides, the corners must be solved before the long sides, and the pattern is counted from corners outward.

Most border patterns have a fixed repeat width. If the design is 100 stitches wide and the border repeat is 12 stitches, the repeat does not divide evenly into 100 (100 ÷ 12 = 8.3 repeats). The solution is either to widen or narrow the central design by a few stitches, or to add a corner section that absorbs the difference. Many chart publishers provide a corner section specifically for this.
Count the repeat width of the border pattern from the chart.
Measure the total border width in stitches (the outside edge length of the whole piece). Divide by the repeat width to see how many whole repeats fit.
If the repeats fit evenly, mark the corner positions on the chart and plan which stitches form the corner. A mitered or squared corner section should be identified before the first side is started.
If the repeats do not fit evenly, decide whether to adjust the central design size or to use a corner that absorbs the spare stitches.
Stitch the four corner sections first. This fixes the endpoints of each side and gives you a reliable landmark to count toward.
Work each side from a corner toward the centre, not from one end to the other. If the repeat does not fill exactly, any half-repeat lands at the centre of the side where it is least visible.

After stitching one side, check the stitch count of the finished side against the chart before starting the next. A count error caught after one side is much easier to correct than one discovered after all four sides are done.

items.symptom: The border does not join cleanly at the corners
items.cause: The corners were not planned before the sides were started.
items.fix: Always stitch the corner sections first. The corner is the fixed point that determines where each side ends.

items.symptom: The repeat is one stitch too wide or too narrow at the midpoint
items.cause: The repeat count was misread from the chart.
items.fix: Re-count the repeat from the chart. Look for the repeat markers (usually indicated by arrows or bold lines on the chart) and count between those markers only.

content.text: A simple geometric border (a repeating zigzag or diamond in two colours) is a good starting point. The repeat is easy to count and the corner solution is usually obvious from the geometry.
